name: Thirunageswaram Naganathaswamy Temple
deity: Shiva as Naganathaswamy, with Goddess Girigujambika; the shrine of Rahu is the principal draw
summary: Near Kumbakonam, this Chola-era Shiva temple is the Navagraha Sthalam for Rahu. Devotees gather for the daily Rahu Kalam abhishekam, where milk poured over Rahu is widely observed to take on a blue tinge as it flows.

sections.history: Sung in the Tevaram hymns, Thirunageswaram counts among the Paadal Petra Sthalams venerated by the Nayanmars. The grand stone temple is attributed to the early Cholas, with Aditya Chola named in tradition as its patron, and it grew across later centuries into an expansive complex. Its name, Naga-natha or Lord of serpents, recalls the belief that serpents worshipped Shiva at this spot. Over generations the temple became one of the most visited of the nine Navagraha shrines, drawing pilgrims who come specifically to propitiate Rahu, the ascending lunar node.
sections.architecture: Built in the Dravidian idiom, the temple presents a stone layout of gateway towers, pillared halls and several sacred tanks, its walls and mandapas carrying the fine sculpture characteristic of Chola workmanship. The sanctum enshrines Naganathaswamy, while the Goddess Girigujambika has her own shrine within the enclosure. The Rahu shrine, set apart for the planet honoured here, is the focus of daily worship and is arranged so that crowds can witness the abhishekam. Subsidiary shrines, corridors and tanks frame a spacious complex shaped by successive additions of the Chola age and after.
sections.legends: The temple's central story concerns the serpents, the nagas, who are said to have worshipped Shiva here, giving the Lord the name Naganathaswamy. As one of the nine planetary temples, this is the abode of Rahu, the shadow planet and ascending lunar node. Devotees carrying Rahu dosha, naga dosha, or obstacles to marriage and childbirth come to seek relief. The best-known marvel is witnessed during Rahu Kalam: as milk is poured over the Rahu idol in abhishekam, it is widely observed to turn a bluish hue while it flows, a sight that draws steady crowds.
sections.festivals: Rahu Kalam pujas are performed every day and are especially thronged on Sundays, when the milk abhishekam to Rahu becomes the heart of worship. Pradosham is observed through the lunar fortnights, and the annual Brahmotsavam fills the temple with processions and ceremony. Around these occasions the streets near the temple take on a festive character, with the Rahu abhishekam remaining the observance most associated with Thirunageswaram.
sections.experience: Most visitors time their arrival to Rahu Kalam to see the milk abhishekam over the Rahu idol and to offer their own prayers against Rahu dosha. The mood is devotional and busy rather than quiet; expect queues at the Rahu shrine, especially on Sundays. Walking the pillared halls and pausing at the sacred tanks offers calmer moments away from the crowd. Priests guide the specific rituals of propitiation, and many pilgrims fold this stop into a wider circuit of the nine Navagraha temples around Kumbakonam.

visit.timings: Open roughly 6:00 am to 1:00 pm and 4:00 to 8:30 pm; verify locally as hours shift with festivals. Crowded during Rahu Kalam each day.
visit.photography: Photography inside the sanctum is generally not permitted.
visit.gettingThere: Thirunageswaram lies about 6 km from Kumbakonam in Thanjavur district. The nearest hub is Kumbakonam; rail access is via Kumbakonam or Thirunageswaram station. The nearest airport is Tiruchirappalli, about 90 km away.
